The probability that a local government unit will establish an intergovernmental joint venture for economic development increases with the level of trust between local government units, the number of other local governments that have already established joint ventures for economic development, the size of the local government unit's economy, the level of economic development in the region, and the level of economic growth in the local government unit.
local governments with more cooperative norms, more trust, and more similar political ideologies are more likely to cooperate.

the likelihood that a local government will participate in a joint venture is positively influenced by (1) its size, (2) its level of economic development, (3) the level of economic development of the region, and (4) its trust in other local governments.

how local governments cooperate in economic development.
how local governments overcome transaction costs to engage in cooperative economic development.
the question of how local government units overcome the transaction costs of cooperation to establish joint ventures for economic development.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cooperation is most likely when local governments are similar in terms of size and political culture, and when they have similar economic interests, such as being located in the same region.
cooperation is not simply a product of the rational pursuit of individual interests, but rather a process in which the institutional context, including norms and trust, is crucial to cooperation.
local governments are increasingly cooperating with each other in order to promote economic development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
local governments can and do overcome transaction costs to cooperate for economic development.
local governments can and do cooperate to address regional problems.
the local context and the presence of endogenous resources are important factors for understanding the formation of joint ventures for economic development.
